# Results — Study 675 (Qstick)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — **Tushar
Chande's Qstick, an N-day moving average of (close − open), measures buying/selling pressure,
and its zero-crosses time a trend** (Chande & Kroll, *The New Technical Trader*, 1994).
Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.
As-of **2026-06-30** (the last complete calendar month; the partial current month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) OHLC for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key), 2005-01-03 → 2026-06-30, 5,406 rows each |
| Fingerprints (`quantlab.repro.data_stamp`) | SPY `c374b2feba04` · QQQ `cd19fe6cb57d` · IWM `cb6689d8b659` · DIA `3a1136ef6422` · GLD `35f763b5047c` |
| Indicator | Qstick = SMA₈((close − open) / prior close) — the per-bar body normalised by the prior close (a documented normalisation for cross-instrument comparability; it never changes the sign of a bar), smoothed with Chande & Kroll's original 8-day window, causal (no look-ahead) |
| Entries | zero **up-cross** (smoothed Qstick negative on *t−1*, ≥ 0 on *t*) — **2,210** mechanical entries pooled across the 5 tapes |
| Timing / costs | up-cross read on the close of *t*, entered at the **next close** (one documented lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per cross |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument trend study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline — exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes.

## The signal — Qstick up-cross vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

The one-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch cross-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = cross − random.

| horizon | n | cross | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (cross−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 2204 | +22.0 bps  | 58% | +3.89 | +34.8 bps  | **−12.8 bps** | +20.0 bps  | −1.68 | 0.094 |
| 10-day | 2204 | +50.6 bps  | 61% | +5.64 | +62.5 bps  | **−11.9 bps** | +48.6 bps  | −1.12 | 0.261 |
| 20-day | 2204 | +92.7 bps  | 63% | +5.99 | +115.3 bps | **−22.5 bps** | +90.7 bps  | −1.52 | 0.129 |
| 60-day | 2194 | +286.2 bps | 69% | +7.25 | +261.7 bps | **+24.5 bps** | +284.2 bps | +0.94 | 0.348 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks decisive (**+5.99** at 20 days,
**+7.25** at 60) — but that is **pure beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index
inherit the drift. Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the Qstick up-cross **loses**
at 5/10/20 days (−12.8 / −11.9 / −22.5 bps) and is a statistical dead heat at 60 days
(+24.5 bps, *t* = +0.94). The cross-minus-random difference **never clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2
bar at any horizon** (max |Welch *t*| = 1.68, at 5 days, in the *wrong* direction).

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — no coherent cross-sectional edge

| ticker | entries | cross | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (cross−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 437 | +77.8 bps  | +2.57 | +117.0 bps | **−39.2 bps** |
| QQQ | 438 | +129.2 bps | +3.60 | +165.2 bps | **−35.9 bps** |
| IWM | 465 | +102.8 bps | +2.60 | +109.4 bps | **−6.6 bps**  |
| DIA | 425 | +62.1 bps  | +2.09 | +82.2 bps  | **−20.1 bps** |
| GLD | 445 | +90.2 bps  | +2.76 | +102.1 bps | **−11.9 bps** |

Every single ticker's Qstick cross sits **behind** its own random-entry baseline at 20 days —
the sign is consistent (unlike the mixed picture in sibling study 473), which only sharpens the
point: the cross isn't randomly noisy relative to the tide, it is a *slightly worse* way to be
long than a coin flip, because it trades less often and still pays the drift's opportunity cost
while it's flat.

## Ordering placebo — scramble the body sequence, nothing changes

Keep the per-bar body **marginal** (same set of close-open values) but permute their **sequence**
before smoothing, so the smoothed series and its zero-crosses become temporally meaningless.

| test | observed Qstick-cross 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY sign-scramble body order | +77.8 bps | **0.814** | 500 |

**81% of scrambled-ordering body series match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.814). The specific
buyer/seller body **sequence** carries no exploitable information — consistent with the
cross-vs-random result above, from a different angle.

## "Just a slow trend proxy?" — the structural check

Qstick_t = SMA₈(close) − SMA₈(open); when the open sits close to the prior close (as it does for
liquid, continuously-traded ETFs), this telescopes toward the trailing 8-day average daily price
change — a **plain trend proxy that never looks at the open at all**,
`mom_t = (close_t − close_{t−8}) / 8 / close_{t−8}`. We test this directly rather than asserting
the algebra: the empirical correlation between smoothed Qstick and the trend proxy, and whether
the proxy's own zero-cross rule does any better than Qstick's.

| ticker | corr(Qstick, trend proxy) | Qstick crosses | proxy crosses | entry-date Jaccard |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | **0.781** | 437 | 401 | 0.201 |
| QQQ | **0.818** | 438 | 410 | 0.222 |
| IWM | **0.818** | 465 | 442 | 0.205 |
| DIA | **0.784** | 425 | 409 | 0.209 |
| GLD | **0.713** | 445 | 426 | 0.151 |
| **mean** | **+0.783** | | | |

Qstick and the naive trend proxy run at **r ≈ 0.78** pooled — a strong structural correlation,
even though the exact crossing *dates* only overlap ~20% of the time (Jaccard), because the
open/close split adds bar-level noise around the shared trend without adding forecasting power.
Confirming the point end to end: the **naive momentum-only cross** (H=20, pooled, 2,080 entries)
scores **+96.7 bps** vs a **+64.7 bps** random baseline — Δ = **+32.1 bps**, Welch
*t* = **+1.99** (*p* = 0.047) — itself just short of the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar. Neither the
open/close split nor the plain price-only version convincingly beats a random entry; Qstick's
extra machinery buys nothing over the trend it echoes.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real lead

Deterministic daily tape: each session's intraday (open→close) return is a latent, mean-reverting
buying-pressure factor (stationary AR(1), half-life ≈ 2 weeks) plus idiosyncratic noise; `edge`
sets the factor's amplitude (`edge = 0` ⇒ pure noise, a fair coin). No self-referential feedback
(that construction was tried and blows up the price path — an explicit engineering note, not
part of the claim under test).

| world | n | cross | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| null (edge = 0), **20 seeds** | — | — | — | mean **+0.07** (sd 1.07), **\|t\| ≥ 2 in 0/20 seeds** |
| planted edge = 2.0 (seed 675) | 155 | +1,385.0 bps | 63% | **+5.12** |

The detector never fires on the null and lights up sharply on a planted lead. *(A
faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The Qstick up-cross does not beat a drift-matched random baseline at any
  of 4 horizons (Δ = −12.8 / −11.9 / −22.5 / +24.5 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; Welch *t* never
  clears ±2, and is negative — i.e. *worse* than a coin — at 5/10/20 days). Every one of the 5
  tickers individually underperforms its own random baseline at 20 days. A sign-scramble
  placebo confirms the body **ordering** carries no information (*p* = 0.814).
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** No residual edge once the drift you were always getting is removed,
  and costs only deepen the small hole. You'd capture the same drift more cheaply — and more
  fully — by holding the index.
- **"Just a slow trend proxy?" — CONFIRMED.** Qstick correlates at *r* ≈ **0.78** (pooled
  basket) with a plain trailing-momentum proxy that never looks at the open, and even that
  simpler trend rule barely (and not reliably: Welch *t* = 1.99 < 2) beats random. Chande's
  open/close split is a laggier read of the same trend, not an independent forecast.
